utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I hope that everyone had a time to -- had a pleasant time at Christmas, and I hope that everyone -- although, the Chamber is fully aware that the circumstances are not the same to everyone in this courtroom, but nevertheless, that you have a good and healthy year 2003. The Chamber has been informed that there are no specific issues to deal with right at the beginning of this first hearing in the year 2003, which would mean that the Defence could call its first witness, which as far as I can see on my list will be Mykhaylo Alex Androvich Tsynchenko. Is that correct? Yes. Then Mr. Usher is trying to locate -- he's gone already -- in order to escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the most recent letter that we have from the Defence, dated 26 December, indicates that the first witness would be Sergij Moroz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have in front of me a letter of the 6th of January, 2003, sent on that same day by telefax, indicating that Sergij Moroz, due to illness, is unable to appear as previously scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the registrar has kindly loaned me a copy of this letter. This is the first time the Prosecution has seen this. I see it's clearly marked to the attention of Mr. Ierace, but neither our case manager Ms. McCreath nor myself have seen this letter prior to today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That raises the next issue, whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simply, we have in front of us the receipts and telecopies dated the 6th of January, 2003, and the same numbers as those we normally and usually use to communicate with the Prosecution. Therefore, the same day the letter was sent and received by telefax, and that is where we stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The usual number is the number of the registry, may I ask you, Madam Registrar, or is it the number of the Prosecutor, the Prosecutor's Office, the OTP? Could you please then -- that number is, Mr. Piletta-Zanin -- what telefax number has been used?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly. We have several numbers in front of us. (redacted), and this one twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Has it been sent to all these numbers or is it -- [Interpretation] was it sent to all these numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite. The last twice, to the last number twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, on what number would you expect to receive telefax messages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to be practical. Is the Prosecution in the position that it could cross-examine the witness which is called right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe the Prosecution could be ready to go, Mr. President, with the perhaps caveat that I see from the letter dated 6 January that the Defence has only two witnesses scheduled for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps depending on the testimony of the first witness, if we might be permitted if necessary a brief recess in light of the fact that there are only two witnesses. That should not present a problem. Perhaps we can take events as they unfold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber would like to be informed about what will be the standard procedure of sending telefaxes, and what numbers will be the numbers that do not create any confusion. So we'll proceed now, having heard the position of the Prosecution, but the Chamber would like to be informed on how the communication technically proceeds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tsynchenko, do you hear me in a language you understand? And what language is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Russian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the translation to Russian functions properly. I do understand that you also speak and understand some English and that you would not oppose against giving a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in English. If you would prefer, however, to do that in Russian as well, then we first have to ask the interpreters to translate the solemn declaration. But if you would not oppose against giving the solemn declaration in English, then I would like to invite you to stand up and give the solemn declaration in English. But if you would prefer to do it in Russian, then please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Tsynchenko Mykhaylo. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Mr. Tsynchenko, you will first be examined by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is it you or is it Mr. Piletta-Zanin who will be examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague will be examining the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: [In English] I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I assume that you can hear me well. The first question that we would like to put to you is the following: Could you in a few words tell us, please, what was your professional background, that is, educational background and your career, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I was born in 1951 in the city of Kiev. I graduated from the Kiev general troop command college, majoring in being an officer of general troops, the infantry, I would say. I served in the Army of the Soviet Union at the positions of the commander of a platoon, commander of a unit, deputy commander of a battalion, officer of the staff of a corps. Then I graduated from the military academy named after Frunze in Moscow. And upon the graduation, I was commander of a corps in different positions Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and management of different level from the army to the military district. And as of 1991, I continued the service in the army of the Ukraine in the Ministry of Defence at the position of the chief or senior commander of the Chief of Staff and head of a unit in the Chief of Staff. As of 1993, November 1993, under the quota designated by the United Nations for Ukraine, I was nominated to the position of deputy commander of a sector of UN troops in Sarajevo, the Sarajevo sector. At that position I was serving until July 1994. After the completion of the term of my stay within the UN troops in Sarajevo, I came back to Ukraine, where I continued my service in the Ministry of Defence, and then I retired into reserve. Currently I'm working in a civilian enterprise or firm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. We are going to focus above all on the period that you have just mentioned, that is, November 1993 up to July 1994. Could you please first of all specify --

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: [In English] -- No translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is translation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let me repeat. Thank you for your comments, witness. We are going to focus on the period from November 1993 to July 1994. You spoke here about the functions you held. Could you tell us, who was - and I expect you to give us the name - who was your direct superior in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, in the hierarchy, I can say that the brigade general Andre Soubirou [Realtime transcript read in error "Simuru"]. Shall I give more names?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Andre Soubirou, brigade general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you perhaps referring to Mr. Andre Soubirou, S-o-u-b-i-r-o-u?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: There was a brigade general, and he had enormous military experience. I know that he's now in the position --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, witness. Excuse me. My question was simply to get the name from you. It wasn't spelled out properly. Was this person, Mr. Andre Soubirou? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: [In English] I can read here. Not Souberou.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact -- I think as a matter of fact if the parties would agree that he's referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Mr. President, let me spell the name of the person that everyone knows. So the name is S-o-u-b-e-r-o-u -- after "B" it's "I." S-o-u-b-i-r-o-u. So we have Soubirou. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For how long was General Soubirou -- for how long did this general hold the position in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I think he arrived approximately -- he arrived from Zagreb the 19th of November. Either 11th or 19th -- or 11th or the 12th. Excuse me. I arrived from Sarajevo and General Soubirou was already in command of the troops of the sector. When I was leaving in July of 1994, General Soubirou was saying goodbye to me. How long he stayed there, I cannot tell. I can only judge from the experience of my colleagues who came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, what was the frequency of the contacts that you had personally and professionally with General Soubirou.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, maybe five times a day or six times a day. Sometimes 12, sometimes for several days we did not see each other, when we were going to different sectors. But practically every day we would meet 4, 5, 6, or up to 10 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you have occasion during your stay in Sarajevo to meet General Galic, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you did have occasion to meet him, was this in a professional context or in some other context?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, that was purely professional encounters which could be happening every day or every other day or once a week. Whenever the situation required that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would you please remind us what was your military rank at the time when you had contact with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, first of all I would like to clarify that my military degree is Colonel. But when I was meeting with General Galic, we would go to personal encounters, when we were talking through liaison officers and through radio stations, we were talking also through our observers and liaison officers. When there were meetings in person, then we would go with General Soubirou.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why did you speak through the intermediary of other officers, witness?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, we were in the staff of our sector, and General Galic was in Lukavica and his staff. That is why we had to make appointments through other officers and we had to talk so that liaison officers would schedule appointments for us, because everyone has his own functions, military functions, and it is not possible just to go there and find General Galic right on the spot immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when did these meetings occur?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just point out. This material is not covered in the 65 ter provided by the Defence to the Prosecution. I just wanted to place that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is on record, since you've mentioned it. I do understand from your remark that it's not your intention to have any oral argument on this issue. We had that before. But you just wanted it to be put on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Especially in view of the fact that we -- the Prosecution did not anticipate this witness earlier on. We may need to make an application for recess before cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may then proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We won't make any comments now. We will proceed immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when these meetings occurred, was there any kind of protocol applied so that officers of a certain rank could address officers of the same rank? Was that some sort of rule?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, if I may, I would like to say a few words about the procedures of service and reaction towards everything that was happening there. Well, the protocol would signify that when we were preparing some bilateral meeting or something official for the meeting. But when it was necessary to solve some issue regarding some cease-fire from one side or the other from within Sarajevo, where I also had a chance to meet with the command at different levels, the commanders of brigades, Bosnian, as well as a chance to meet at levels of commanders of brigade at the other side. So we had very quick response to various circumstances where I was sent by General Soubirou whenever there was need for intervention. This is why no protocol was envisaged -- protocols were taken or held only at official meetings in the government. There was mostly meetings by General Soubirou, by our political adviser Viktor Andreev and also General Rose and they had meetings with the Prime Minister and the president of Bosnia Herzegovina. Also, whenever they would go to Pale and have meetings with the commanders of the troops from the Serbian army and the president of the Republika Srpska. Then we had official protocols or minutes of meetings were taken. As far as I know, no official minutes of meetings were taken at other level meetings or no protocol was envisaged. I was present at a number of meetings. I don't remember how many meetings, but usually General Soubirou would always hold negotiations in person with General Galic. I would come with him together, but I would work at my level usually with the Chief of Staff or with his officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the screen I see that we have a translation problem. I think it has been restored now. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think you said that -- you asked the witness to allow you to stop him, and you told him that -- to come to the core of your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're having now translation again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you specify the following: When these discussions occurred, was there any kind of protocol in the sense that the discussions were between equals? For example, from one general to another, from a colonel -- between a colonel, between two colonels, between two majors, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I can say only that General Galic preferred to meet with General Soubirou. I can also quote him. He said, "We are generals. We will talk to ourselves. And you, you are a colonel, so talk to my colonels." Well, as far as protocols are concerned and no protocols or minutes were taken. Usually after the meeting, General Soubirou would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I will interrupt you. Should I understand your testimony being that General Galic addressed you at least once saying "you are a colonel, so I won't talk to you. Talk to my colonel"? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: That's right. Those were his words verbatim and I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know whether General Galic applied this protocol as a general rule, yes or no? Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Not quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether in general General Galic respected these protocol rules; that is to say, "I am a general. I only want to speak to another general," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please specify the question to the extent --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- To the witness whether this protocol was always applied as far as he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Mr. President, for the sake of the transcript, your question wasn't entirely reproduced in the transcript. I don't know if we have technical problems of some kind here. But I have noticed that on occasion certain elements are missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It might be due to the fact that I spoke when translation was still going on. I will not do that again. But I asked you to specify the question to the extent whether the witness could tell us whether this protocol was always applied as far as he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In this case, I won't paraphrase you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the question. Could you answer it.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: When we went to see him in order to solve any problem, together with General Soubirou, with his assistant Major Bergeron, together with our officers, perhaps, we could meet with General Galic when his officers were present as well. If we needed to solve a problem and we came only two of us, then he would normally just remain with General Soubirou and discuss the problem with him. I wasn't quite sure what you -- what was the gist of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But I think you've answered the question perhaps even without realising that. Thank you. I would now like to turn to a different subject, witness, and I would like to examine the issue of destruction. You spent -- you lived for about six months, a little more than six months in Sarajevo. Could you tell us where destruction was caused to buildings in Sarajevo, as far as you can remember, where the majority of the destruction was caused.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: The largest destruction was in the area close to the airport. There were checkpoints there. I hope I'm using the right word, "checkpoints." There were Bosnian and Serbian checkpoints. That area was fully destroyed. There was not a single building intact there along the road. There was large destruction in the area of the bridge over the Milatska river in Grbavica, and in the area of Ilidza. Many buildings were destroyed there. In addition to that, high-rise buildings in downtown Sarajevo were destroyed as well. These high-rise buildings were destroyed partially. Some floors were destroyed, especially on the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth floors. These floors were not inhabited. In addition to that, the area near the stadium was also destroyed, the stadium that was used during the Olympic games for ice sports, such as hockey and ice skating and so on. In addition to that, there were -- there was some destruction visible on the outskirts of the city in the mountainous area. As one would leave the city and head towards the mountains, one could see certain buildings destroyed there. If you would give me a map, I would be able to point out these areas for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. In a minute we will show you a map, but first of all I would like you to specify a few issues. You spoke about areas close to the airport. Do you remember the names of these areas?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: If you would give me a map, then I would be able to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: -- A map later. You spoke about the higher storeys of high-rise buildings, the sixth, the seventh floor, et cetera. Why were these buildings or these floors, why were they not inhabited and why were they damaged, at least partially?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, that's quite understandable. If there was some kind of an exchange of fire, then it was a guided fire, and these floors were targeted. There were no windowpanes on those floors. And one could see, for example, a floor with apartments on it and one could see through the apartments on that floor, because this was a direct fire. All of this took place before I arrived. When I arrived in Sarajevo, this -- examples of destruction were already present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, witness. In the outskirts that you mentioned, since you spoke about the airport area, did you have the opportunity to move to the centre, to move around the centre of the town, that is to say, the old centre, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Certainly. We went everywhere. We went -- I personally went everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you went to those areas, to the old centre -- when I say "the old centre," I'm referring to what we call the old town, the Stari Grad, that area. What can you tell us -- could you please wait for me to finish the question, please. What can you tell us about the state of the buildings, the state of the property in that part of the town, that is to say, in the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: In the downtown area, the theatre building was destroyed, fully destroyed. In addition to that, the library building, which was considered as one of the most important buildings in town before the war was also destroyed. It was a rare example of that type of architecture. And then there were some areas that were damaged, not destroyed. There's an area in that part of town where there are three temples. There was an Orthodox church, a Catholic church, and a mosque. All of them were damaged but not destroyed. In downtown, in every building there were residents. They lived on lower floors or in the basement area, but almost every building was inhabited. It is difficult now for me to pinpoint exactly which buildings were destroyed and which were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For the French translation, uninhabited -- no, I apologise. I apologise. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I'd like to turn now to the buildings in the old centre, witness. Was the extent of damage comparable, yes or no, to what happened at the conflict lines themselves? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: The extent of the damage is something that I cannot describe to you now because I did not take any notes. I didn't take any footage. There was a lot of journalists there who recorded that, and I believe that the extent of damage is well known. Therefore, I wouldn't like to go into that. But most of the buildings that were destroyed were located along the areas where there was combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one question, one precise question: In Sarajevo, did you see any religious sites, such as mosques, that had been totally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: No. No. There were no completely destroyed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like you to tell us, and then we'll show you a map -- could you tell us where you lived while you were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I lived in the PTT building, which is a building where the sector headquarters was located. I hope the PTT building is a sufficient depiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what you could see from your windows. Or for the English booth, which direction did your windows face?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I faced the mountains, the mountainous area. Well, if we take that this was the area where I was, this is where the PTT building was, and it faced the mountains, just as I am now facing the distinguished Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The west?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: North.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I think we could now show you the map with the assistance of the usher. Thank you. It's Exhibit D1819. It's the same map that we are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we could put it on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise the map that we can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Just a minute, please, because I can't see it very well here. I think that this here is the PTT building --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Just a minute, witness. You can't point to it on your screen. You have to point to the map on your left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For the Russian booth, I didn't say what you just said, but that's not that important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the PTT building. So from my window, I faced Vitkovac, that area. This is what I could see from my window.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you point to that again, please. Could you please point to the PTT building so that we can see that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: This is the PTT building. And I faced Vitkovac. I could see Vitkovac and this area here, the elevated area. This is what I could see from my window.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness, for the sake of the transcript, pointed to the building that bears the inscription "PTT" on the map, and he then pointed to the area which is to the north, north-east, let's say, beyond the Miljacka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What can you tell us, witness, about what you could see from the window of the PTT building in the direction that you indicated? And I'm referring to weapons. Which weapons could you see?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Practically no weapons. I couldn't see any weapons from my window. I could see explosions, fire exchanged in Vitkovac area. The explosion and the fire mostly originated from the centre of Sarajevo. I could see that. As to the weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps I'll rephrase that question. Do you know whether the forces, the interior forces that are sometimes called the presidency forces, do you know whether they had heavy weapons, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: They certainly did. They certainly did have heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. I think the witness has already answered the question and then this is an attempt to prod the witness on further.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all. But I don't think that the witness answered the question. The witness answered the question that I put to him concerning what he could see. I'm not asking him about what he could see, but I want to know what he knows, which is a different matter. And apparently the Prosecution fail to realise this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed. You may answer that question, whether you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- knew whether there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What do you know about the heavy weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has already been answered, I think, by now as a response to your question, but -- the answer is, "They certainly did. They certainly did have heavy weapons." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since you said that the presidency forces had heavy weapons, could you tell us what comes under this definition, under the definition of "heavy weapons"?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, if you talk about the definition of the "heavy weapons" -- well, I can tell you as military, and I can tell you as this definition would include any weapons of calibre over 12.5 millimetres. Anything larger than a large calibre heavy machine-gun. These are mortars. Those would be guns. Those would be tanks, the self-propelled vehicles or all other types of artillery and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. Thank you. You mentioned mortars. Did you ever hear mortars being fired in Sarajevo, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, witness, do you remember any particular occasions on which you could have heard mortars being fired while you were in the PTT building, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I heard such shots both within the building and also during my rounds across the positions. That was one of my functions during the line of conflicts, and also I could see -- and I can point at the map -- that the line of confrontation -- it was in this area, in this area there were some shots. And I can tell you that from both sides I could hear mortar shellings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'll interrupt you there. Let's stick to the exchanges of fire or to mortars being fired. You told me that you had the opportunity to hear mortars being fired from the PTT building. Is that correct? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Both inside the PTT building and also when I was going in that area. I both heard and I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But my question now concerns only what you could hear and then see from the PTT building at a given point in time. Were you able to hear mortars being fired and see something from your windows which faced the north, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what this concerns.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you only one thing, is that when we -- for more than two months - and not only we but also the force of Mr. Akashi, de Mello, and Victor Andreev and all others - when we all tried to make the truce happen and the receive cease-fire happen. There were cases of provocations both from the Bosnian side. And there were -- some open provocations were take place, the open of fire was provocated. And from the PTT building, it was -- in that area, where there were two or three instances like this I can tell you. On this occasion General Soubirou would meet with the commander of the corps, of the Bosnian corps, and there were several shots. And on the Serbian side they had good intelligence, rather good artillery intelligence, which would notice such things from under the building of the PTT those things were happening. And I can tell you that my window was facing on the side and there was -- I had a balcony and there was also a staircase, which would go down to the back door or it was also called the back staircase. And there there is always a French soldier on duty from the commander's corps and he was always observing these things. And after these shellings I remember there was a time about 2100 or 2000 or 8.00 p.m. or 9.00 p.m., when the car came and within about 400 metres from the PTT and fired -- and made an assault -- and made a mortar shot towards the Serbian side, and immediately that soldier knocked on my door and said, "Excuse me, sir. We have such a situation." And I saw a car leaving. And I am saying that this was a purely Bosnian thing because closer to PTT -- we had PTT security from the UN side and also further on there were police stations. That is why no cars, civilian or any other type of cars, could be operational in that area at that hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You used the term "a car," a vehicle. Did you see that vehicle with your own eyes? I'm talking about the vehicle connected with the mortar being fired. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I saw a car leaving. It was a Toyota. It was a pick-up type of a car. I didn't see the fire -- actually, I didn't see the fire from that car, but that was the only car on the street and that was leaving from that side. And then the commandant came and nothing could be found on the spot from which such a shot could be done. Then the only possibility that such a shot could have been fired from within the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How much time went by from the moment you saw that vehicle and the firing of the mortar, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, the observation was constantly held, and they were -- there was a person on duty who was taking observations, so that person that, soldier, made the observation and then he would run to my door. I think it would take about 30 seconds to come to my door and knock at the door. Then I'd come to open the door. It would be about 30 seconds. He said, "Sir, I heard a shot." Then he was speaking French. He didn't speak any English. And then he pointed to me at that car, and I saw the car leaving. The car had lights off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. At the spot that you were observing, was there anything else perhaps? That is, any fixed mortars that may have been there? Yes or no? Let me rephrase the question. The moment the vehicle left the scene, did you see on the spot where it had been any weapon, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you now have this map to your left in front of you. Could you please indicate to us the places that you mentioned as being especially badly destroyed at the time. First of all, pointing them out with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if we could move the picture to the south a little bit and enlarge it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More, more. Further down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, speaking about the badly destroyed -- the series of destructions, I could tell you that they took place in that area, that's road toward their field.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is making a circle round the area called Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, there are some private residential houses. Well, it's hard for me to name the district because I can't see the name of the district here. But here is the road from this intersection towards the entrance to the air field. All these private houses were destroyed. The area of Ilidza right here, was also destroyed. There were serious destructions in this area. A major destruction also took place in the area of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You are not finding your way on this map. We'll give you another map straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But for the transcript, the witness has also pointed on the map to the area of Ilidza, which is to the left, more to the left.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. In this area there was the line of contact --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, so as not to waste time, I'll interrupt you there. I'd like to show you --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence counsel was in fact leading the witness. At the time he mentioned the word "Ilidza," the witness was not pointing to that area. In fact, he was just roaming around all over the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just try to shortcut this. The witness started indicating the area which is indicated Ilidza, and then later on he also pointed at an area just north of what seems to be a yellow major road just north of the name Ilidza in red, just as he pointed previously when Mr. Piletta-Zanin was referring to Nedzarici, to a wider area but of which the centre reads in the map as "Stupsko Brdo" two times and "Stupsko Brdo" again, that creates approximately a circle, just south of a major intersection indicated in yellow colour. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, we are going to distribute the second part of this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, briefly, do you recognise this map, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please focus on this map, if you can. And if you can see the area indicating the zones which in your opinion may have been destroyed to a major extent.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, to a major extent I can tell you that was destroyed the zone of Grbavica. In this -- on this side of the Miljacka River. And then on the other bank of the Miljacka River, there was the line of separation -- the zone of separation between the Bosnian and Serbian troops. That was the line of contact. And next to the cemetery there were major destructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. I do apologise. The witness is pointing with his pointer to the Grbavica area situated to the south of the Miljacka River, that is, the area that is indicated on the map with the word "Grbavica," close to the symbol of a hospital. Witness, since you also mentioned here the front line along the river, I'd like to ask you another question: Do you know or did you know at the time whether in the town of Sarajevo on the side of the presidency forces there were factories or workshops producing weapons?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: According to the data which we had, we knew that there were two or three workshops which were producing mortar mines and guns, mortar shells and tubes. I cannot tell you specifically, but that's what we heard. I cannot confirm that or overrule that, although these things were spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say that you heard about them, what were your sources of information?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, the UN and the staff of the battalions and both the French and the Ukrainian and other battalions, next to them we could see a lot of people who were feeding on them, those people who had no work, no means for survival. That is why personal contact was always established with people -- with such people. Confidential relationships were established as well. And probably that's where the French battalion -- there were some intelligence officers working in such milieus, and I believe that they received such information from such sources, which was later reported at different levels. But I cannot tell you who and where specifically he got such information. I believe that such workshops did not require any specific equipment to be established. I think it takes about two or three drilling machines, and that's about it. You don't need anything else, and I guess you just need to relocate it -- you can relocate it in two or three hours easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, leaving aside for a moment this question of weapons workshop, I should like to come back to the question regarding destruction. Apart from the area of Grbavica that you have just mentioned, did you have occasion to see other areas close to Sarajevo on the Serb side which were also destroyed, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, practically pursuant to my job functions, once a week I would go around the whole front line from both sides, both from within and from the outside, both from -- in those areas and from the side of the Serbian party. The destruction on the line of contact was from both sides. That is why to say -- some destruction I don't know what to say. So some buildings were destroyed indeed. Those buildings which were out of range of mortar or tank fire, those buildings were intact. Well, I can tell you that from both sides there were some destructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we take the break, I think it will be at half past 3.00 or perhaps later, at a quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you speak about artillery, do you have -- could you give us an example of the spot that was destroyed that was relatively far from the front line. And I am referring to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: The basis of our visits to the Serbian side were the requests and protests made by the Bosnian side. They complained that there was shelling going on and various other things, and this is why we would go to the Serbian side in order to resolve the issue on putting an end to such incidents, such as shelling and so on. This is why I visited the Serbian side more than once. I visited their hospital, which was in a totally destroyed village, quite far from the front line, some 12 to 15 kilometres, in fact. I was shown that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I apologise for doing so. No, no. I have to interrupt you for reasons of time. Do you know the name of that place, of that location, locality?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember it now. All I remember is that there was the only -- the only building that was left intact there was either a school or a church, and they set up a hospital there with some 60 patients. I remember that there was a little girl there without legs, and I remember that during my visit there was a surgery -- a man was operated on who had an abdomenal wound. The people that worked there were a lady from France and a French physician as well, who were members of Medecins Sans Frontieres. They worked there as volunteers. They were she would during their work. They basically --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you on either of these maps that are to your left pinpoint this particular spot on the map, or at least the direction in which it could be found.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: This was along the road leading to Pale in the Serbian territory. It was in that direction, but I can't tell you exactly where because I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness mentioned on the map to the south the road leading towards the municipality of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness. I'll come back now to purely technical questions. Did you have occasion to see in Sarajevo or in its environs mortar craters? Please answer with a yes or no. Mortar craters.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: You mean the craters? Yes, certainly I saw them. There were many craters, on both sides. The war went on. People were attacking each other, so there certainly were craters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have occasion to see mortar craters in other places outside Sarajevo during your personal military experiences, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Certainly. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of this personal experience that you had, both in Sarajevo and elsewhere, did you ever see during your personal experience a crater left by a mortar which contained within it, dug into the soil, hard soil, dug into hard soil, the final part of the mortar known as the stabiliser, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: If I understood you well, are you in fact referring to stabiliser that are visible from the ground, that remained visible and are stuck in the ground? Am I understanding you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question is the following: We are talking about a hard surface like asphalt. We are talking about what is called a stabiliser, that is, the tail of a shell. Is it possible -- can you tell us, on the basis of your experience, whether you have ever seen a crater that contained the stabiliser dug into the ground at the bottom of the crater itself? Yes or no? Have you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with that phenomenon, and I saw it several times. However, those were shellings with mortars used in training, without explosive material in it. Stabilisers can fall as far as 5 to 7 metres from the crater, depending on the angle of fire, also depending on the calibre of the shell, the distance from which it was fired. If it remains visible there, that means that there was no explosion at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would like to make things quite clear. We are reading in the transcript that you did see this phenomenon several time; however, only during training, when firing was done without explosive material. Is that how I should understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. The witness said "I'm familiar with the phenomenon." He didn't say he had seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said that you're familiar, does that mean that you have seen such stabiliser fins embedded in the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only in Yugoslavia, but in other hot spots where I went on tour of duty I saw artillery fire, mortar fire, and let me just explain this. When there is an explosion, a shell explosion, then stabiliser cannot remain in the ground. It cannot get stuck in the ground. And this can be verified very easily. If you fire in a training field ten shells from a mortar, you could see this for yourselves. Only it would be as likely to happen as somebody surviving the airplane crash from 10.000 metres. I personally don't believe this to be possible. The stabilisers can remain visible only if this is a training shell, a training shell that penetrates the ground and the stabiliser remains visible in the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question to you was whether you had seen this stabiliser fins in the ground as a result of a training session, whether this was your personal observation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When using training shell, I saw this once when I was undergoing training myself and a training shell was used without explosion material in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps you could find a suitable moment to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps that moment could be now, as we are moving to another line of questioning later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. One of the booths asked me to make longer breaks for technical reasons. I just wanted to inform you of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, does the name Zetra, does it mean anything to you? Does it remind you of anything?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, this is an area in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please, if it's possible for you to indicate this on one of the maps, could you point to it. But I should add that we need the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please show the west map, that is to say, the number -- yes, you've got it. You've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you point to the place called Zetra on this map.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness complied and he pointed to a building bearing the name Zetra close to the sports complex in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, what can you tell us about incidents that may have happened close to this area called Zetra and incidents that you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, in the area of Zetra, I can tell you that the French battalion was stationed. It was stationed right in that very building where an ice skating rink was located for figure skating during the Olympics. And from the stadium in the area of Zetra, we were dispatching helicopters and we were receiving helicopters with civilian population from the area of Gorazde, those who were wounded. So when we came there, we organised there some aid and further treatments and dispatchment from the area of Sarajevo. In the area of Zetra, I can tell you that I came to visit that battalion six or eight times. During my service there, I can tell you that there were two French battalions. One was the marine battalion. I don't remember its exact name. And one battalion was from the Foreign Legion, the French Foreign Legion. One French soldier was wounded in the area of Zetra, and this was practically my time. I had an encounter with the commander of the battalion. And according to the order from General Soubirou, I was inspecting the positions and posts, and this soldier was wounded by sniper fire. At the time pursuant to an order from General Soubirou, in every battalion special anti-sniper groups were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you there. And it's just for the sake of time. You said that this soldier was wounded by sniper fire. Could you please use the pointer. And if you know this, could you indicate the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, if I had an exact plan of the location of that battalion at the moment, then I could. But at the moment I can tell you only that we would come -- or I should say I would come to the battalion by this road. There was an entrance here. And this was the entrance to the battalion. And in front of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise. I'd appreciate it if you could use the pointer to indicate the direction of fire. Where did the fire come from, on the basis of what you were able to see or on the basis of what you were able to discover later on.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, the sniper fire was being led from this direction, I should say, the south-east direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we enlarge the image. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the basis of this witness's knowledge on this fact has not been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you just pointed to a direction. I'll go back to that. But what personal knowledge do you have of this? How did you know this? Why? Et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, together with the commander of the battalion, we were staying in his office, and from his office he had -- before the Olympics there was a restaurant constructed. Which was not operational, of course, in those days but it was intact. It was not ruined. And it was being used by the French battalion as a canteen. And on top of the canteen, there was a terrace. If I may say so, it had a small fence made of bricks. It was like a fence -- it was used for observation, as an observation place for those who would come there. We immediately came to that terrace, and on that terrace there was the anti-sniper group, and there were two French soldiers, one observer with binoculars and one had a rifle, anti-sniper French rifle with a tripod, a large calibre. And the sniper, according to the report, was eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you now tell us, from what direction fire was opened. Could you indicate this. Could you show us on the map.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you from exactly where the fire was coming, but I can tell you exactly that the anti-sniper group with a special directional gun was staying at this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness pointed to an arch, which starts at Zetra and extends in a south-westerly direction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please take a felt tip that the usher will provide you with.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The witness pointed south-easterly view --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Easterly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's exact. That's exact. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please use the felt tip to trace the arch that you mentioned, what we call the firing arch.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now concentrate on other questions. We no longer need the map at this stage. As assistant to General Soubirou, did you ever see a written protest which was forwarded directly to General Galic concerning one or several sniping incidents, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: No, I have not seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, as General Soubirou's direct assistant, if such form of protest had been lodged, would you have been in a position to be aware of this fact, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, some issues were beyond my competence. But if such a written protest were presented, then I would have known about this for sure because General Soubirou was holding daily meetings and such protests or demarches were always presented to officers on duty. As a rule, all the protests for both parties were transmitted through the radio station or through the telephone communication or through the radio station. This was the main operational chain of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. Thank you, witness. Should I understand that for the six months or more that you spent in Sarajevo you never saw such written protests at your level? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly at the moment because a lot of operational paperwork was -- had been taken place, and quite possibly one of the paragraphs in one of the papers could be -- could be containing some kind of a protest. That's quite possible. But I cannot tell if there were some official protests or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: One question to you, witness: Were you ever present at meetings with General Galic during which he would have been forwarded such written protests concerning one or more sniping incidents, precise and identified sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: No. Specifically in the written form I never saw such protests in meetings with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we are now going to move on to another subject. In general terms, how would you describe the personality and the competence of General Soubirou?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, first of all, from my side this would not be very ethical to do that because I was his deputy. But I can tell you that General Soubirou was very experienced and well prepared general and he had vast combat experience and vast experience in running the troops. He was decisive. He would take decisions quickly and adequately. He was not frightened. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As a result, should I infer from this that if -- I'll withdraw that question and rephrase it. Should I infer from this that if there were facts which justified a protest to be made to General Galic, then General Soubirou would not have failed to react?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall at the moment such instances. I know that after the shelling of Sarajevo he would go to General Galic and General Soubirou would talk to him. But whether this was on paper or not, I cannot tell you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, with the assistance of the usher, I would now like to show you an exhibit. The number is 1821.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there is an R number on the document. I don't know whether this document is disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution and whether this would cause the -- any party to ask for --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, our case manager is checking right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can't see a name. I can't see any names that would cause a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it might be a document -- a document that needs protection for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It has been lifted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been lifted. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, do you recognise such documents? Do you recognise the form?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is a general document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would like to read the second paragraph under number 1. This is what we are interested in, and it concerns the question that I shall put to you. I'll now quote in English: [In English] "Areas most affected were the centre of town GR 9059, Stup GR 8459, Grbavica GR 9059. Tank activity was observed in GR 855, and I think "9" or "8." "The majority of the activity is believed to have been directed at front line areas approximately 80 per cent." [Interpretation] In this text, we can see that tank activity has been mentioned. Witness, did you see any tanks in Sarajevo? And if so, where?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, the term "tank activity" does not signify the usage of tanks. Tank activity is -- signifies that tanks were moving in that area. An observer who witnessed that reports in his report that observed some tank activity. This does not signify that he observed firing from tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't mention fire being opened from tanks. My question is whether you yourself saw any tanks. And if you did, where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I saw two or three times tanks inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us where you saw these tanks.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: In the area of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you see any in the centre of the town, or rather, in the part of the town in the so-called presidency's hands?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question has been answered. I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: A minute ago you said -- you mentioned Zetra, which is located close to the Kosovo area. Do you know if there were any heavy weapons near the Kosovo zone, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I cannot tell you specifically about Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In that case, I'm going to ask the usher for his assistance. He will show you a second exhibit, number 1822. Thank you. Do you recognise the form of this document, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to read the first paragraph to you, under item 1, "General assessment." And I quote: [In English] "Sarajevo remains unstable. The shelling was again at a relatively low level. Areas shelled that are considered on/near the confrontation line were Stup GR 8458), Raljovac (GR 8460), and Vogosca (GR 8764, 8765 - Vice 9765, BSA side)." [Interpretation] Witness, with regard to these locations, could you, first of all, confirm what has been stated in these two -- in these several lines, that is to say, the shelling of these locations.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Shelling of those areas -- when there is a shelling going on, be it daytime or night-time, then usually the areas close to the front line are shelled, and they could have fired shells into the air. But regardless of that, observers would record that and report that there was a shelling going on. Therefore, these were daily typical reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, was there any possibility of error in the registration of these shellings and activities which led up to this report?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: It is very difficult to specify the source of fire and the direction of it. Therefore, an observer could have made a mistake, the observer that recorded the fire. The observer usually indicates just the area of fire. But in order to pinpoint it accurately, an observer -- it would have to be a trace bullet in order to pinpoint the exact area or source of fire. If any other ammunition was used, it would be very difficult to calculate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: With respect to this type of document, witness, we frequently come across the expression "mixed rounds." Could you tell us in technical terms, military technical terms, what was covered under this term "mixed rounds."

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I can't tell you what this means. It could mean that an observer was not very competent, the one that used the mixed rounds phrase. It could mean that there was mortar and gunfire at the same time, and perhaps this term was used when there was both mortar and gunfire simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, witness, there is no classical or uniform technical definition of the expression that I have just used.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like with the assistance of the usher once again to show the witness Exhibit 1823, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, looking at the clock, I see that you have approximately 10 to 15 minutes left from the time estimate you gave. And if I look at the list of exhibits, then of course I am aware that you started only in the latter part of the examination of the witness with the exhibits. But would you please stick to your estimates, as far as time is concerned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As always, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since time is counted, it would be kind enough if you could try and answer with a yes or no as far as possible. First of all, do you see the period covered by this exhibit, and could you read it out for us? It is the third line of the document.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: This document pertains to the period from the 10th to 11th of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please look at the very first line and read -- or rather, it will be the second line, and read the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it frequent for such apparent errors, if it is an error, occur on such documents, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: No, not frequently. However, it did happen occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, let us concentrate now on the first paragraph of point 1, "General assessment." Once again, and I shall quote what it contains in English now. [In English] "-- the past 24 hours have been a steady increase in the general level of activity, particularly in the use of indirect fire weapons on both sides. Areas most affected have been Stup GR 8459, Central Sarajevo GRS 9059, 9159, Zuc all along the -- I think, confrontation line. Grbavica and Alipasin Most, GR 8559, 8659." [Interpretation] Excuse me. Now, with respect to indirect weapons, could you tell us, if you know, what were the calibres that the presidency forces had at their disposal. And we're talking of mortars.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: They had 40-millimetre mortars, 66-millimetre mortars. I think they also had 82-millimetre mortars and also 120-millimetre ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think -- no, I'll stay with this document for a little longer. This document in the third paragraph of point 1 speaks of snipers, Bosnian snipers. My question is the following: Did you ever hear within the framework of your military activities in Sarajevo that presidency snipers were used by presidency forces? My question first. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Snipers were used on both sides, both by the Bosnian side and the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Did you ever hear mention made of the use by presidency forces of snipers against targets situated within the lines controlled by the presidency forces, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. Do you mean to say that the Bosnian snipers fired on targets that were located in their territory? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That was my question, yes, whether you ever heard such things being mentioned. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: First of all, this was a war that could be described as a semi-guerilla war, guerilla war being fought by the Bosnian side. It was very difficult to exercise control over any group of people. It was quite possible for any group of people to shoot within their own territory. If they had an argument amongst themselves, they could have fired -- or opened fire within their own territory. There were cases like that, not only on the Bosnian side but also on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I should now like to go back to something I mentioned a moment ago, with regard to the professionalism of General Soubirou. I shall read to you something that I have already given to the booth, which is a document originating from the Prosecution. And please bear in mind what I'm reading conforms with what I -- what is written. General Soubirou said in an interview --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May we see a copy of the document. We haven't received a copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I have a copy here. It is Exhibit ERN 01100499. And we also have a copy for the Chamber, but we do not intend to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sentence that I would like to read --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Informing the witness that this document originated from the Prosecution. I don't know what this document is. It's just a --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just withdrew that statement, but we're still speaking about the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution no longer recognises its documents, and this, I find, disturbing for the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. My point is this document has not been tendered by the Prosecution by way of evidence. That's completely different. This may have been an interview conducted by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be -- let's be practical. I do understand that the Defence indicates that this is a document that has been disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution and is referring to the number. I also understand that the document will not be tendered into evidence. So therefore, unless there's any specific part, please, you could, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, draw out and shift to a certain part. But why not just put a question apart from any document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is only a single sentence that I would like to read. And according to the old rule that is in force, we will save time. And I intend to do that. The sentence is the following -- may I do it, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually if you use a document, even if you do not tender it, it's usually on the list. But I do not see this document on the list. Could you indicate just by -- so that we can first read and also Ms. Mahindaratne can read the part that you would like to quote --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the first sentence, Mr. President, the first line.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is one and a half lines long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The part that starts with "I got." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the witness be asked to remove his headphones for this portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the witness does understand some English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't quote it. I won't quote it, Mr. President. I won't quote from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, General Soubirou said something to this effect: Speaking of General Galic, he said, probably in French, that I have the impression that he was removed because he was not hard enough, because he tended to demonstrate compassion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you say that you're not quoting, I take it that you do not quote. So please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I didn't quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have almost literally repeated what is said there, and that is unfair after you indicated that you would not quote, because if you change one or two irrelevant words and say I'm not quoting any more, then you are playing tricks. And please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be glad to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know if General Galic was removed from his position for any particular reason?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I asked you to move to your next subject and not to stay with the same subject. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
