utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. Let me consult with my colleague. Wait, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will proceed as follows. Unfortunately, we believed that we had the possibility to prove something that we were not authorised by your Chamber, though it was a very important point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just briefly respond to that. And I will ask the witness to take off -- do you understand any French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Could you take off your headphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] You had the opportunity to ask this witness whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President. Your pardon for interrupting. The witness can read English, so perhaps he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [In English] Oh, yes. Yes. Then we have -- Mr. Usher, could you please change the channel of the witness. [Interpretation] The Defence did have the opportunity to ask the witness whether he knew the reasons why General Galic was removed from his position and had the opportunity to confront the witness with a reply that may have been given by another person, that is, General Soubirou. So you did have the opportunity to do this in a way that would not lead the witness towards a particular answer, and you did not take advantage of that opportunity but you chose to follow a path which is not acceptable. Therefore, will you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue, Mr. President. Thank you. I think, nevertheless, it is sometimes the duty of the attorney without seeking confrontation to state clearly that the Defence considers that it is in a position not to be able to continue and that its rights have been violated, and we say so with great respect. And therefore, we have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may put his headphones on again. Ms. Mahindaratne, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness or at least to start to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We -- we should definitely be able to start and perhaps might conclude today itself. But may I seek a very short recess before we start, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many minutes would you need? Five minutes? Would that be --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes? Let me just have a look at the clock, if we would have a break for ten minutes now. That would bring us to quarter past 5.00. That would be too long. Perhaps we will have the shorter break now and grant 20 minutes. We'll resume at 25 minutes past 5.00 and have no other break any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Good sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit D1823.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, this document was shown to you by learned Defence counsel and you examined it. Would you please examine paragraph 2, which I will read to you. "Bosnian school came under direct mortar fire at 1030 hours resulting in a number of casualties." It's reported in those words in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're referring to paragraph 1, I take it, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Paragraph 1, which is -- 2 I did say, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then the second linear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm referring to paragraph 1. I beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, and the second sentence. It's reported to such effect. Now, during your period as deputy commander for sector Sarajevo, were you privy such incidents? Did you learn about such incidents or did you read reports about civilians being subject to direct mortar fire in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I would like to clarify something here. It was not a school which was -- which came under direct mortar fire. And mine --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- Interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a rule which says that while a witness is about to give information, he should not be interrupted. And this time I see that he was interrupted just as when he was of his own accord going to give information about the school, which seems to me to be rather important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just first read the question again. Yes, you may proceed your answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My objection was based on the fact that I asked him a completely different question. I asked the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But part -- the part you read was, "The Bosnian school came under direct mortar fire." Part of your question was to learn about such incidents or did you read reports about civilians being subject to mortar fire in this manner? So you're referring to what is described in the report. And if the witness wants to explain what he understands the report would be. Otherwise, he cannot answer the question about such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed with your answer. You started telling us that you'd like to clarify something, and you said it was not a school which was -- which came under the direct mortar fire. Could you please there continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A mortar mine detonated on a playground not far from a school, and at that moment there were children playing there, and there were some casualties among the children. There were several killed and several wounded. Such reports when civilians were subjected to mortar or artillery fire or gunfire or rifle fire or sniper fire, I heard about them and I read about such things, and there were casualties both from the Serbian side and the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. If I take you back to paragraph 3 on that same document. I will read it to you. It states: "Attacks on UN personnel, equipment --" And then thereafter it says: "A number of small arms rounds hit the PTT building during the night. One of them penetrating the UN HCR radio room window narrowly missing a civilian."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I withdraw that, Mr. President. I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown document -- Exhibit number 1822 -- I'm sorry, I think it's 1821.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could take you back to the final paragraph. It's paragraph number 1, but the last sentence. It's recorded: "Small arms activity was evident around the PTT building, and on two occasions rounds hit the building itself. One round entered the UNHCR radio room narrowly missing a civilian, and there is a record of rounds. Bosnian in, 105 mixed rounds; Bosnian out, 25 mortar; Serbian in, five rounds; Serbian out, 61 mixed rounds," says such a report. Sir, would you agree with me that generally, like this type of report, you could agree that the outgoing rounds from the Serbian sector is far in excess of the incoming rounds to the Serbian sector?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult to tell you specifically with regard to what is meant by "in" and "out," because on one day there could be outgoing shells from the Serbian side. On the other day, a lot could be coming from the Bosnian side. So this was a war taking place. It was not just walking around. The fact that PTT was being shot at, this is true. My room was shot at, I can tell you. A large-calibre bullet penetrated through my wall. It was a direct penetration. It went across my room and hit the opposite wall. This is the answer to your question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How would you conclude based on this particular report which has been shown to you by the Defence, at least with regard to this particular day on which -- with regard to which this report has been issued?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you anything on this issue for the reason that at that moment I was no longer in the Sarajevo sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm merely asking you to respond on this report. Now, you did in fact -- your testimony was that you were in -- you were the deputy commander of sector Sarajevo from November 1993 to July 1994. This report is for the period -- for the date 11th January, 1994, so you were in fact still the deputy commander sector Sarajevo. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, this is so. But I can tell you that the work of a deputy commander did not imply only my constant stay in the building of PTT. I was on a mission in Zuc. I was on a mission in Gorazde. I was head of those missions, and I could be for two or three weeks away from that building, if you understand me. So I simply do not recall this incident when this was taking place. There were firings going on quite often, and nobody took that seriously. One shell was shot at PTT from the firearms. Well, nobody paid much attention to that. All the windows which were facing on the outside from the PTT building were blocked by sacks with sand.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, sir. I'm under a time constraint. Is it your position, then, that you cannot speak to the incidents about which the reports -- the reports relate to which were shown to you by the Defence? And I'm referring to documents D1821, 1822, 1823. Is it then your position that you do not know personally about those incidents, that you have no recollection of those incidents? That's your position?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: No. Please understand me correctly. The fact that a shot came to the window of the radio room does not signify that this is a big incident which took place. This just means that it was noted in the daily report. And two days later nobody would even remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If that be the case, sir, how is it that when I questioned you about the incident where a Bosnian school had come under fire, which was referred to in document number 1823, you seemed to remember that particular incident in vivid detail, to state -- to give, in fact, details about that particular incident? How is it that you remember about that particular incident and not the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, when the shelling at the Alipasino field took place and children died, then about 40 minutes right after that shelling I was on the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you were -- you were personally a witness to the shelling of the children in Alipasino Polje. That is your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I saw with my own eyes the results of the shelling. I witnessed the results. I did not witness the shelling, but I witnessed the results of the shelling. I saw that the children were killed and that there were children who were wounded. I do not remember the exact number. I think about six or seven children.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the map, I think 1820 and 1819. If the witness may be shown map number 1820 first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you drew a line going from north to a south-easterly direction. What did you indicate by that line?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to indicate by that line that when we and the commander of the French battalion came to the anti-sniper group, then the direction of the weapons of the anti-sniper group was directed in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So in other words, that line indicates the location where the anti-sniper groups were positioned. Is that correct? That's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Not exactly. A line cannot depict a location of the anti-sniper group. The line shows in which direction the weapons of the anti-sniper group were directed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you point out where the group was positioned on that line. On which side?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: In the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And from there, it is your position the line indicates in fact where their weapons were directed at. It was not a line of fire which you indicated.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: No. When we jumped out and we saw that their weapons were directed on that side, the weapons of the anti-sniper group, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, weren't you still the deputy commander of sector Sarajevo when the anti-sniper agreement was concluded on 14th August 1994?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It was concluded by UNPROFOR with the two warring factions; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you yourself involved in the process?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then you would be aware of -- were you aware of the fact that UNPROFOR and particularly General Soubirou had to take -- there was much effort on his part to convince the Serbian army to agree to the -- or to concede to the agreement? You would then have been privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, practically everybody at the level of Sir Rose; Viktor Andreev, who was political advisor, Diana Nikola [phoen], who was advisor to the General Soubirou; General Soubirou himself; the commanders of battalions, everybody was taking at their level all the efforts in order to convince the two parties to stop the fire and sniper activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As part of this agreement, there were two teams called operations -- anti-sniping operations teams and anti-sniping interventions teams --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, may I first interfere for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tsynchenko, right at the beginning of your testimony you told us that you held the position in Sarajevo until July of 1994. You're now asked by Ms. Mahindaratne whether you were still serving in Sarajevo when an agreement was concluded at the 14th of August, 1994, and you responded in the affirmative. That's at least what I read on my screen. I have some difficulties in understanding how you can stop serving in July 1994 and still serve on the 14th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was not serving. Maybe I did not understand the translation or the interpretation, rather. Let us put the question again, if possible. What was the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please try to clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of the anti-sniper agreement concluded by UNPROFOR in August 1994? Are you aware of such an agreement?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I am aware of such an agreement because this agreement was being prepared not in a couple of days. This was work which took at least half a year on both sides until this agreement came into being. And if -- even if I was not there at that moment, my subordinates still were there, who later reported to me in Ukraine when I was in Ukraine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When did you leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I left Sarajevo in July of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would that be the case then, sir, that you were not in Sarajevo or you could not have been party or privy to the conclusion of the anti-sniper agreement which was concluded in August 1994? Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If that be the case, sir, how is it that you just described in detail about convincing parties to enter into the agreement, so on and so forth, which you just stated earlier on, when you were not in fact -- in fact party to the -- or privy to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object for two reasons: Firstly, the witness just said that it took six months to arrive at some point. And the second reason is - and this is important - we don't see why we're speaking about this agreement so much, which is outside the time frame of the indictment, which goes up to August 1994, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about August 1994. But -- and let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it was after the 10th of August, 1994, and it doesn't appear clearly -- it didn't appear clearly in the English translation, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you please rephrase your question to the extent that the witness has told us on how the parties had to be convinced of entering in such an agreement but give no detail whatsoever about the agreement itself as it finally was made and -- nor about the implementation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you said that the agreement was negotiated for about six months prior to your departure -- from about six months before you departed Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: To come back to my previous question, were you then aware of the attempts and efforts taken by UNPROFOR to convince especially the Serbian side, the Serbian army, to enter into the agreement? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I was familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In that you agree there was difficulty in getting the Serbian army to agree to the anti-sniper agreement.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I know about that. There were difficulties not only regarding the Serbian side but also regarding the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, sir, that it was specifically more difficult to convince the Serbian army than the presidency forces to enter into the agreement? Isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence knows that leading questions are not admissible [as interpreted]. But there is a certain way of formulating a question, something that is tendentious in the question, if we look at the other replies that the witness has already given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leading includes a certain tendency -- the witness has earlier responded that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just reading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there's just one matter. I didn't say that leading questions weren't admissible. I said the opposite. And this is not clear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The English transcript is not correct in this view because you said that they were not -- you were aware that leading questions in cross-examination were not inadmissible. Ms. Mahindaratne, the witness testified that they had to convince the parties to enter into the agreement. I think that's the starting point for your --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will withdraw that last question in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of anti-sniper groups in existence in Sarajevo prior to the conclusion of the agreement just concluded in August 1994? Were there anti-sniper groups before that?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Anti-sniper groups were established in two French battalions prior to the conclusion of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly. If you wish, I can give you an explanation so that things become quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, sir. Was it before you -- were there anti-sniper groups in existence when you arrived in Sarajevo, or were they grouped in such manner after you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I believe that anti-sniper groups were established in each battalion prior to my arrival. I mean, the French battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So it is your position that these groups were in existence when you arrived in Sarajevo in November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: They existed. But if you allow me, I will give you a more detailed explanation. Commander of each battalion is responsible for his soldiers. He's responsible for security of his soldiers. Therefore, there were special anti-sniper groups in French battalions from their very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So the anti-sniper groups that you're referring to, which you say existed prior to August 1994, were set up by battalions to protect the personnel of the battalions. Is that your case?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The anti-sniper groups established after August 1994, the agreement of -- which was negotiated while you were in Sarajevo, were --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. Objection. We spoke about groups established after August 1994; that is to say, after the time frame in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you explain to us what relevance would be of what happened after the 14th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I'm -- I was merely going to ask the witness about what was negotiated. In fact, the groups, where they were to be located during the course of negotiation, what transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're talking about -- not about the agreement but you're talking about the negotiations -- the content of the negotiations --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that finally led to the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you said you participated in the negotiations leading to the anti-sniper agreement which was concluded in August after your time, 1994. You did participate in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Then would you be able to -- are you aware of where these groups were mainly to be located? Where were the anti-sniper groups and the teams were to be located?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the exact location, but region-wise weren't the teams to be positioned inside the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: In order to understand what I'm trying to say, you have to have military education. A group can be located today in this particular room. Whereas, tomorrow it can be transferred to a totally different part of the town or to the front line. Therefore, one cannot put it in the terms that you are trying to put it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to answer the question. The question was whether during the negotiations anti-sniping groups were discussed to be positioned where, within the city or also - that's, I think, the question - also on Serbian-held territory or exclusively on BiH presidency-held territory. That's the question first. What the reasons might have been for that is a different matter. Please first answer that -- respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain to us why you can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said. The preparations for negotiations and the agreement itself is not the same as signing the agreement. Any shelling or any sniper activity entailed us travelling to Lukavica, to various other regions where we held negotiations. The negotiations were held first with the presidency forces and then with the Serbian side. And this was basically our daily activities, both of General Soubirou and myself as the first deputy, as well as political advisors and deputies of General Rose, so this process of negotiations lasted quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was: Have anti-sniper groups been discussed to be positioned -- to be positioned at both sides of the confrontation line? Has that been discussed? Or has it been discussed on one side? And if so, on what side? I'm talking about what has been discussed, not about what finally was agreed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. Discussions, any discussions, were always held with both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that was not my question. My question was whether the discussions of setting up anti-sniping groups were discussed as setting up anti-sniping groups on both sides of the confrontation lines or just on one side of the confrontation line, and if on one side of the confrontation line, on what side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that this is something that I cannot tell you, because I simply do not remember. I cannot recall the exact details. However, I know for a fact that discussions were held with both sides. I took you to mean that you needed to know the exact locations of anti-sniper groups. I don't know that. However, discussions were held -- all discussions were held with both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that the negotiations that led to the anti-sniper agreement, which was in fact concluded in August 1994, related to establishment of anti-sniping groups within the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Including the city of Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you do in fact know the locations where the groups were in fact -- in fact to be positioned.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: No, I don't know locations. I don't know those locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown the map D1820. May the map be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated -- you testified about a village you visited --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke of a location where you visited in the Serbian side, to use your own words, where you had visited a hospital which was totally destroyed along with the village, and you indicated on the map that particular location or the road leading to that location. Can you please point that out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not state that. He didn't indicate on the map, as far as I can remember -- he didn't indicate this village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My recollection is he indicated in what direction it was. But perhaps you could ask him again -- you could ask him again to point at the direction that he did before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, would you be able to indicate on that map that particular village?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't show you that exact village. I don't remember that. I simply showed -- indicated the road which led in that direction, leading -- the road leading to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, my recollection is that the witness testified that the village was between 12 and 15 kilometres from the confrontation line. If you can find on one of these maps any location which is at a distance of 12 to 15 kilometres from the confrontation line, then please ask the witness to point at the village. But if not, it's no use.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, how far on that road would one have to travel to get to this particular village you spoke of? How far on the road you indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question isn't clear. From where? From where?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will withdraw that. I will withdraw that. In the interest of time, I will withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the maps be returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke of General Soubirou conducting meetings with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It was your position that you participated at such meetings only when officers of General Galic were also present.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. There were several such meetings where general questions were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Accordingly, General Soubirou had met General Galic in your absence many times.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. This is quite natural.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did General Soubirou discuss with you about every item of correspondence that left his desk, or did he show you such correspondence every time such document was issued by him?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did he discuss with you about the contents of all the meetings he conducted with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: To a question from the Defence - and I will repeat it to you verbatim - "were you ever present at meetings with General Galic during which he would have been forwarded such written protests concerning one or more sniping incidents, precise and identified sniping incidents?" And your response was, "No, specifically in the written form I never saw such protests in meetings with General Galic."

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The question was, sir, with regard to written protests. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was it the case that protests were sometimes made in the course of discussions?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Have you yourself made such a protest to any person?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I made some protests to commanders of brigades, both at the Bosnian side and at the -- I mean, at the presidential side and the Serbian side. We made such protests in Zuc, we made such protests inside the city. This is quite natural. This is daily, routine work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you made protests to -- commanders of the brigades of the Serbian side, how did you convey your protests? What did you tell them? You do not have to say it verbatim, but what type of protests were these?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall it word for word, of course, but we would say something like this: From your side there came some shelling, although we have come to a cease-fire arrangement. And the answer would usually be, "We have also been fired upon," and I could never find the truth from any side. And to any protests we would hear in response that, "We have been also fired at and we were firing in return."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, when you use the word "firing," do you also include shelling as well as sniping?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Those would be firing as from -- from mortars, from firearms, and including the sniper firings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: About how many such protests did you make to the commander -- the brigade commanders on the Serbian side during the course of your tenure in Sarajevo? If you cannot remember, it's okay. Or if you can, give an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, this is impossible because practically if such incidents were taking place, then immediately we would respond to such incidents. This could be happening even two times a day. It could be once a week. I cannot tell you -- count this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So it would be -- I beg your pardon. It would be too many to quantify.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Right. And the presidency side -- but I can say the same about the presidency side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, to a question from the Defence counsel - and I will repeat this verbatim - "as a result, should I infer from this that --" no, it goes on "should I infer from this that if there were facts which justified a protest to be made to General Galic, then General Soubirou would not have failed to react?" And your response was, "Well, I cannot recall at the moment such instances. I know that after the shelling of Sarajevo he would go to General Galic and General Soubirou would talk to him. But whether this was on paper or not, I cannot tell you this." Sir, were you in saying "General Soubirou could talk to General Galic after shelling of Sarajevo," were you present at such discussions personally?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, now I cannot recall at the moment. I was present at a number of discussions. I had my own functions. For example, I was collecting the Serbian weapons when the agreement was reached. I was collecting those arms and the weapons we were placing with the security guards from the outside. Next to every point where there were heavy weapons, tanks, mortar weapons from the Serbian side. And the Bosnian weapons heavy weapons were collected inside Sarajevo in the Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said that you were sometimes present when General Soubirou discussed issues with General Galic. Isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did those discussions also include shelling of Sarajevo, which you have referred to in your testimony earlier?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, there were such negotiations as well. There were negotiations on the conduct of convoys, whether humanitarian aid, that they did not get detained on the way. We he would negotiations on the work and transportation of civilian doctors. We also discussed the question of water supply to Sarajevo and the reconstruction works were discussed, the removal of the construction and the removal of trash and debris. All these issues were discussed constantly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you refer to the words "there were such negotiations as well," could you elaborate more as to how shelling of Sarajevo was negotiated. In what sense did you mean negotiated with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object because in the answer given by the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think it might be prudent to ask the witness to remove his headphones and perhaps -- or turn it to another Translation Unit since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please change the channel, since you are still speaking French, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll continue in French, Mr. President. First of all, I object a posteriori to the question put by my learned colleague for the following reason: The witness has already answered regarding the shelling that he referred to that he was not present at that meeting between Mr. Soubirou and General Galic. That is the first point. The second point is that when talking about negotiations, many things are covered: Humanitarian aid, convoys, et cetera. But never negotiations on the object of the shelling. And the question that has been put in continuation by my colleague implies that there were negotiations on the shelling, which is not correct. And on those two bases, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, we have a problem unless you also start speaking French. But if --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, all I can say is that the transcript clearly shows the continuation of the questions and answers, which leads to my -- this particular question. I have not in any way misled the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I may assist, Mr. President. If I may assist, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: From the question: Did those -- you said that you were sometimes present to that point -- from that point onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That's -- could you give us a line and a page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't know whether -- I don't know whether it's the same. Line 22 on my page, page 67. I don't know whether my numbering here on this PC is the same as yours, Mr. President. It's the third question before the objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne. No, we are looking a bit more back in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The pages seem all to be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you also repeat your source you gave me. I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 67 -- I beg your pardon, Mr. President. Page 67, line 22. It starts at, "You said."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at page 67, going on to page 68, the answers seem not to be unambiguous. So the Prosecution is allowed to seek confirmation of how it understands the answer, but in a prudent way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I beg your pardon, Mr. President. If I may just take a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you a question in this manner. I will repeat it to you. I referred to the discussions conducted by General Soubirou with General Galic where you were present. And referring to such discussions where you were personally present, I ask you this question: Did those discussions also include shelling of Sarajevo, which you have referred to in your testimony earlier? And your response was, "Well, there was such negotiations as well." You said so, sir. Now --

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I would like to say --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I haven't asked you the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you clarify as to how shelling of Sarajevo was negotiated by General Soubirou and General Galic. How did -- what was the contents of the discussion? I don't expect you to answer in verbatim sense, but if you can just say what took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Apart from the fact that the term "negotiation" I find shocking, I wonder whether you also answered -- responded to my objection a moment ago when I was explaining the question of the bombing, the shelling that we are still referring to, that the witness already gave a negative answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please point exactly on where the negative answer was given, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I cannot, because on this model of computer I am very inefficient, even more so than with others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. Mr. Tsynchenko, you have talked -- you have testified about meetings where shelling was discussed. I'm not talk about negotiations, but where shelling of the city was discussed. You said that such meetings took place. Have you ever been present during a meeting where shelling of the city was discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to clarify with your permission. I was present mostly at those meetings -- I was constantly present and mostly at those meetings when we were discussing the issue of -- the conclusion of an agreement on the cease-fire, on the collection of the firearms which cannot be transported out of the area, and also those areas which -- those weapons which can be brought outside the Sarajevo zone by 20 kilometres. This involved a lot of technical issues and a lot of meetings were held at various levels, and I was -- I personally was responsible and was nominated by General Soubirou -- I was nominated as the responsible person for those issues and I personally would go to those areas and would fly there by myself and with him to those points to places where we would collect armaments. This was a long negotiations process. We held meetings at the highest level. We held meetings between Mr. Akashi and Mr. Rose, and Sergio de Mello also participated very actively in this process. So I was present mostly at such types of meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was: Were you ever present at a meeting where shelling as such was discussed, the shelling of the city that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that protests, both concerning shelling and sniping, were almost made at -- on a daily basis. Would you consider such protests not to be a discussion on shelling or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was mostly oral protests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So to that extent, shelling was often subject of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not think that it was very often that the level of General Galic, these things were discussed with him. But with his subordinates, with the chief of staff, with the artillery commanders, this issue was discussed much more often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So mainly on the lower level and sometimes with -- in meetings with General Galic as well. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, to a question from the Bench just now you answered, "I do not think that it was very often that at the level of General Galic these things were discussed with him." Now, you clearly testified, sir, that you did not participate in the meetings between General Soubirou and General Galic constantly and it was only some meetings where General Galic's subordinate officers were present, that you were present. Isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If that be the case, how could you so ultimately state that such things were -- that you don't think that such things were discussed at the level of General Galic because you did not in fact participate in those meetings. Isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, I did not get the substance of the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you did not participate at most of the meetings conducted between General Soubirou and General Galic or between General Galic and other senior officers of UNPROFOR. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which other senior officials? You mean General Rose and ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Viktor Andreev?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: No, that was not my level.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore, you would not be able to say or state as to what transpired at those meetings. Isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: At the confidential level, no, I could not say. But approximately which issues would be discussed at those meetings, I would know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What made you say that shelling was not discussed so often at the level of General Galic, especially in view of the fact that you did not meet -- or you did not participate at those meetings so often?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to clarify. General Soubirou was not always himself in the Sarajevo sector. General Galic was in command of his corps and was not always as well in that area. In order for a meeting to take place, it was necessary to organise that meeting. If these were daily contacts, then nobody would be in command over any army and nobody would be taking care of any other business except for going and visiting each other and holding meetings. I would say that active exchange of meetings were taking place when we were talking about a cease-fire and collection of armaments. These meetings were taking place very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony was that General Soubirou met General Galic in your absence. That was clearly your testimony. Wasn't that the case? Or if I may rephrase, you did not participate at all the meetings conducted between General Soubirou and General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Of course not. This was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to chief of staff of General Galic with whom you said shelling has been discussed, in addition to brigade commanders. Do you know the name of the chief of staff of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't remember exactly his name but I remember he was a colonel. I think a lot of time has already lapsed since then, many years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have contact with him?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did have contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In saying that shelling was discussed with the chief of staff and the brigade commanders, did you also yourself make such protests to the chief of staff of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to say protest, because no written protests were handed over. We would come over and we would say, "Another shelling or firing has taken place from this and that area on Sarajevo." And I cannot simply explain how this would work. It's not that I come over and I say, "I would like to protest, or to launch a protest." No, we were -- we came to talk and to discuss the issue of the cessation of fire activity, and this process was going on for a long time, because both parties were not -- were rather reluctant to reach the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So you prefer not to use the word "protest." Let me ask you in this manner: Did you discuss shelling of Sarajevo with the chief of staff of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, we did discuss that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Often?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Not very often, no. Well, the system was a little bit different because liaison officers were working in most instances who had constant meetings, and every one of them had his own functions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You said that you made sometimes daily, sometimes twice a day, and sometimes weekly protests to the brigade commanders about shelling of Sarajevo. You personally made those protests. You said that in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I did not make such protests personally, but this was done by UNPROFOR, by those commanders of battalions which found themselves at the line of contact with that party.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony was that protests were made by you to the brigade commanders. That was your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I didn't mean myself personally. I meant commanders of battalions and officers of the Sarajevo sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could my colleague cite the place where exactly the witness made this reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think in French I heard you say that he personally made this protest, but that were not the words of Ms. Mahindaratne. She said that you did it, and I think she got a clarification for that. So unless you insist. But it was the answer that the witness testified that he did not personally make these protests. But it was not the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you know the -- would you be able to identify these brigades of the Serbian army to which these protests were made by UNPROFOR about shelling of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I don't remember the names of brigades. Do you have a map, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you don't remember, that should be all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No more questions, Mr. President. That concludes cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Yes, Mr. President. Are we continuing up to 7.00 or quarter past 7.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, certainly not to quarter past 7.00. We'll continue to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have some eight or nine minutes left because of the tapes, so we'll certainly finish at five minutes to 7.00, not one second later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a minute ago, in response to a question put to you by my learned colleague, a question that -- which concerned your response in relation to Zetra, you said that the line that you traced on the map did not indicate where fire was coming from but it indicated the direction that anti-sniper weapons were pointing in. Do you remember stating this? It's page 74, line 4 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, if you indicated that these weapons were pointing in that direction, then my question is as follows: What were these weapons pointing at? I'm referring to the anti-sniper weapons.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: They were pointing to the direction from which the sniper fire originated. Weapons cannot be directed to any other side except the side for which the fire is originating. I just wanted to be very specific in giving my answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for this answer. Have I understood your testimony correctly: The line that you traced on the map marks both the direction in which anti-sniper weapons were pointing and as a result also the direction from which fire was coming. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, I would now like to go back to certain other issues. You spoke in response to a question from the Prosecution about the school in Alipasino Polje. I don't know whether you remember this, but for us it was page 53 approximately. Do you remember the answer that you provided then?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: I said that that was not a school but a children's playground in the vicinity of a school. At the time, there were children there. That was around 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you, the UN forces, ever carry out an investigation into this incident? I'm talking about a technical investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. This is not an issue that comes out from cross-examination, about an investigation into a shelling incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you tell us where investigations of shelling incidents were dealt with in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, obviously there is no direct relation to the question of investigations, but the Prosecution did raise the issue of the shelling of a school -- the issue of a shelling that we didn't mention. To the extent that this issue was raised, I think that it is Defence's right to ask whether investigations were carried out, because one of the important issues is to know whether the information came through and if so, how. I have to admit that I can -- I am no longer able to use my computer, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether that causes the problem, but I will allow you one question. But please direct it in the relation you just indicated. So the question was about the details of what happened in the playground near a school and so investigations in that respect. I'll allow you to ask questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to this incident, do you know - yes or no - whether investigations were instigated with regard to this incident? And if so, what might have been the result of these investigations?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was an investigation carried out after every incident. I know that for a fact. As to the conclusions that were reached after that investigation, I can't tell you anything because the experts that led that investigation came from the staff of General Rose. There were some French experts there, British experts as well. We did not have our own experts in the Sarajevo sectors that could have carried out such investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. As far as two other questions that were put to you by the Prosecution and which concern the number of protests lodged, you said that there were numerous protests. I'm referring to page 65 and 66. So my question now is as follows: When you say that there were numerous protests that were made, first of all what did this concern as a general rule? And secondly, did this concern protests made against just one of the parties or were the protests made in relation to both sides?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that last question has already been answered in a previous moment, so the first -- it's my recollection that you said that protest was made to both parties. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you then please answer the first part of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both sides -- that's right, both sides lodged protests. And as to the other question, I'll explain why there were numerous. Because when one reads the reports, one can see that there was firearms, fire, mortar fire, and so on. And commanders at various levels lodged in such protests almost on a daily basis; therefore, I can't say that General Soubirou went to see General Galic daily in order to lodge in protests. I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Part of the question. I'm looking at the clock and keeping in mind the tape. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have also noticed that, Mr. President. I have another three or four questions, unfortunately. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to do this as efficiently as possible. But tomorrow morning I think ten minutes would be certainly enough for three or four questions -- tomorrow in the afternoon. Yes, of course. I'm making a mistake. Mr. Tsynchenko, we'll adjourn until tomorrow. I don't think it will take much time tomorrow in the afternoon, presumably not more than half an hour to three quarters of an hour. Yes, we'll adjourn until tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. May I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you're about to give tomorrow, not with anyone, not with the parties, with no one. We expect you to be back tomorrow at quarter past 2.00. It will not take very long, I take it. We'll adjourn until tomorrow in the afternoon, the same courtroom, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
